questions.enonce_markdown:
Define the following terms as used in ecology:

(i) Pollutant.

(ii) Afforestation. *(2,2 marks)*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) **Pollutant:** any substance (solid, liquid or gas) or form of energy that is **added to the environment, usually by human activity, and is harmful to living organisms** (or damages the environment), e.g. smoke, sewage, oil, pesticides.

(ii) **Afforestation:** the **planting of trees** (establishing a forest) on land that **has no forest cover / was not previously forested**, to restore or create vegetation cover.

questions.enonce_markdown: State the harmful effects of bush burning. *(5 marks)*
questions.corrige_markdown:
- **Kills organisms:** destroys small animals, insects, eggs and the soil micro-organisms (decomposers and nitrogen-fixing bacteria).
- **Destroys habitats** and food of animals, so biodiversity falls.
- **Soil damage:** humus and organic matter are burnt, so the soil loses nutrients and fertility; bare soil is exposed to **erosion** and leaching.
- **Air pollution:** smoke and carbon dioxide are released, causing respiratory problems and contributing to **global warming**.
- **Loss of vegetation** and economic loss: destroys crops, forest products and property, and reduces the water-holding capacity of the soil.

questions.enonce_markdown: Describe the flow of energy in nature. *(6 marks)*
questions.corrige_markdown:
- The **sun** is the original source of energy for almost all ecosystems.
- **Green plants (producers)** trap light energy by **photosynthesis** and change it to chemical energy stored in food (carbohydrates).
- This energy passes along the **food chain** when the producers are eaten by **primary consumers** (herbivores), which are eaten by **secondary consumers** (carnivores) and then **tertiary consumers**, e.g. grass $\rightarrow$ grasshopper $\rightarrow$ frog $\rightarrow$ snake.
- Only about **10 %** of the energy is passed from one **trophic level** to the next; the rest is **lost as heat** in respiration, in movement, in excretion and in parts not eaten or not digested.
- When organisms die, **decomposers** (bacteria and fungi) break down the dead matter and release the remaining energy as heat.
- The flow of energy is **one way** (it is not recycled), which is why food chains are short, with few trophic levels.

questions.enonce_markdown:
During a bush burning exercise, the quantity of carbon dioxide released was estimated and measured at regular intervals as shown in the table below.

| Time/minutes | 0 | 5 | 15 | 25 | 30 | 35 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\mathrm{CO_2}$/litres | 0 | 10 | 30 | 80 | 70 | 50 |

Draw a graph to represent this information. From the graph, determine the amount of carbon dioxide that will be released during the $10^{\text{th}}$ minute. *(5 marks)*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Graph to draw (on graph paper):**

- Title: *Graph of carbon dioxide released against time during bush burning.*
- **x-axis:** time / minutes, scale e.g. 2 cm to 5 minutes (0 to 35). **y-axis:** $\mathrm{CO_2}$ released / litres, scale e.g. 2 cm to 10 litres (0 to 80). Both axes labelled with units (the independent variable, time, on the x-axis).
- Plot the six points $(0,0)$, $(5,10)$, $(15,30)$, $(25,80)$, $(30,70)$, $(35,50)$ with small crosses and join them with a smooth curve or straight lines, starting at the origin. The graph rises to a **peak of 80 litres at 25 minutes** and then falls.

**Reading at the 10th minute:** there is no plotted point at 10 minutes, so draw a vertical line from 10 on the time axis up to the graph, then a horizontal line across to the $\mathrm{CO_2}$ axis. Between $(5,10)$ and $(15,30)$ the graph rises $20$ litres in $10$ minutes (2 litres per minute), so at 10 minutes:

$$10 + 2 \times (10-5) = 20 \text{ litres}$$

**About 20 litres of carbon dioxide** (accept 19 to 21 litres from a curve).
